web_evidence.title: A Widow for One Year by John Irving | Literature and Writing | Research Starters
web_evidence.note: The signed research article explicitly says the novel is told in omniscient third person and describes the later narrative as divided chiefly between Eddie and Ruth.

web_evidence.title: Finding the Way Back: A Widow for One Year
web_evidence.note: A scholarly dissertation chapter repeatedly identifies Widow's omniscient narrator, including its access to characters' thoughts and its narration across the novel's three arcs.

web_evidence.title: Renewal and Resilience
web_evidence.note: The review describes Irving's omniscient narrator across all three parts, including flash-forwards and knowledge unavailable to the characters; it separately identifies interpolated chapters from fictional books.

web_evidence.title: BETWEEN THE COVERS
web_evidence.note: Barbara Kingsolver explicitly identifies Irving's omniscient point of view while distinguishing the base novel from embedded samples of works supposedly written by its characters.

person_note: The Goodreads passages repeatedly show a nonparticipating narrator moving among Ruth, Eddie, Hannah, Harry, Marion, and other characters, entering private thoughts and projecting into their futures. Independent scholarly and major-review sources explicitly identify an omniscient third-person narrator across the whole novel. First-person material in q00130, q00133, q00155, and q00156 is local speech, reflection, or character-authored material; web sources confirm that the novel interpolates fictional works by its writer-characters, so these passages do not create sustained first-person base sections. No credible evidence of alternating base narration was found. The main residual limitation is the absence of a sustained authorized excerpt, but the convergent quote, scholarly, and review evidence is sufficient for high-confidence THIRD.
